easy.q: President Christofferson said that, with a sense of duty, he would speak about one subject. What was it?
options: Gambling
Going into debt
Wasting time on phones
easy.why: He said he felt compelled, like the prophet Jacob, to speak boldly: “So, with a sense of duty, I turn to the subject of gambling.”

easy.q: President Christofferson shared President Hinckley’s very short answer to the question about gambling. What was it?
options: It is fine now and then
We are against it
Each family may decide
easy.why: President Hinckley said he could answer the question about gambling very briefly: “We are against it.”

easy.q: According to President Christofferson, what has made gambling available almost anywhere and at any time?
options: The television
The newspaper
The smartphone
easy.why: He taught that the smartphone changed gambling from something that needed a trip somewhere into something available “continuously, privately, and almost anywhere.”

easy.q: President Christofferson asked us to stay away from gambling. What did he plead that we do with the time and money we save?
options: Use them for doing good
Spend them on safer games
Keep them all for ourselves
easy.why: His plea was “not only to refrain from gambling but to use the time and resources saved thereby for doing good.”

easy.q: At the very end of his talk, President Christofferson shared a prayer about gambling. What did he pray for?
options: That we will gamble only with our friends
That we will not treat gambling lightly
That we will gamble only small amounts
easy.why: He said, “I pray that you will not treat gambling lightly,” and ended with the prophet Jacob’s words: “O be wise; what can I say more?”

medium.q: Why did President Christofferson say he felt “a bit like” the prophet Jacob as he began?
options: He had been asked to speak on very short notice
He was speaking mostly to his own family
He felt a duty to speak boldly on an unpleasant subject
He was nearing the end of his years of ministry
medium.why: Jacob felt compelled by the Spirit to address subjects that were not edifying, using “boldness of speech.” President Christofferson felt the same duty about gambling.

medium.q: According to President Christofferson, what is the larger concern with gambling, beyond losing money on individual wagers?
options: Constant mobile access can turn occasional play into a costly habit
Gambling companies may close and keep their customers’ money
Players may be cheated by games that are secretly unfair
Large winnings are heavily taxed in most countries
medium.why: He warned that continuous, mobile access can turn occasional entertainment into repeated behavior that “displaces saving, increases debt, and creates far-reaching family and social costs.”

medium.q: President Christofferson quoted President Oaks on “opportunity cost.” What does that phrase mean in this talk?
options: The fee a person pays to have a chance at winning
Time spent on one thing is opportunity lost for another
Prices go up when many people want the same thing
Good chances come only to those willing to pay
medium.why: President Oaks taught that “if we spend time doing one thing, we lose the opportunity to do another.” President Christofferson asked what gambling makes us give up.

medium.q: Why did President Christofferson bring up the Apostle Paul’s counsel about food sacrificed to idols?
options: To show that those strong in faith need few cautions
To show that early Saints faced harder tests than ours
To show that what we eat matters as much as what we spend
To show that our casual choices can lead a weaker person astray
medium.why: He applied Paul’s words this way: “Since your recreational gambling may lead a weaker brother or sister into temptation, just don’t do it.”

medium.q: Why did President Christofferson say gambling is hard to reconcile with the commandment to love our neighbor as ourselves?
options: The time it takes leaves little room for serving those around us
The money it uses up could otherwise have been given to the poor
Whatever one person wins has to come out of someone else’s loss
The secrecy around it slowly weakens trust within a family
medium.why: He taught that gambling is built on wanting something for nothing, and “its structure requires that any gain comes at others’ expense.” He said that is hard to reconcile with the commandment to love our neighbor as ourselves.

hard.q: A journalist quoted in this talk noted that only a small share of gamblers become compulsive. Why, in his words, is that still alarming?
options: Experts believe the true share is far higher than reported
A small share of tens of millions is a very large number
That small share includes nearly all young gamblers
Those few account for most of the money that is lost
hard.why: The journalist wrote that the small percentage “becomes a very large number when tens of millions of [people] suddenly have casinos in their pockets.”

hard.q: Which situation best fits President Christofferson’s caution to those who feel strong enough to gamble only for casual fun?
options: A longtime gambler hides growing debts until the savings are gone
A student sees betting ads at every game and feels pressure to join
A new member sees a respected leader place a small bet and follows
A worker declines the office betting pool and is teased for it
hard.why: He asked the strong to consider their example. Those “newer or weaker in the faith” are watching, and a little gambling may cost them more “if they take license from your example.”

hard.q: Because our resources are stewardships, President Christofferson said the question about a purchase goes beyond whether it is legal. What is the further question?
options: Whether it will return more money than it first cost us
Whether most people around us would approve of it
Whether we could afford it if all the money were lost
Whether it builds anything in us, our families, or others
hard.why: He taught that the question is whether a purchase “builds anything—in us, in our families, or in those around us.” Gambling, he said, produces nothing of value.

hard.q: A man reasons that he bets only with friends who can afford to lose, so no one is hurt. Which teaching of President Oaks quoted in this talk answers him most directly?
options: Seeking to take from others without giving value harms the taker’s own spirit
Friends who can afford a loss today may find themselves in debt tomorrow
Small bets among friends are where compulsive habits most often begin
Most people who gamble end up losing far more than they had planned
hard.why: President Oaks asked, “What does gambling do to its participants?” The attitude of taking “leads us away from the giving path of Christ” and is “destructive of spiritual sensitivities.” That harm falls on the one who takes.

hard.q: President Christofferson said gambling, “even for fun,” leads in the opposite direction from something. From what?
options: The financial independence that careful investing brings
The prosperous, just, and equitable societies that work builds
The friendly rivalry that sports are meant to create
The carefree rest that a day away from labor provides
hard.why: He taught that a life well-lived supports and rewards work: “Work leads to prosperous, just, and equitable societies. Gambling, even for fun, leads in the opposite direction.”
